title: Document that docs/log.md does not preserve authored prose, and warn at sync time
description:
docs/log.md's CONTENT contract is undocumented, and a careful consumer built a test against the wrong expectation because of it.

parseEntries (src/core/log.ts) is total by construction: any line that is neither a folder heading nor an entry -- prose, a stray hand edit, the `# Change log` title, a blank -- is SKIPPED. A regenerated log is therefore a function of git history plus the entries still legible in the old file, and nothing else. Hand-authored prose placed in docs/log.md does not survive `lore sync`. That is deliberate, and the reasoning is good (the alternative, failing the sync, would leave a repo unable to run lore sync at all because of a file lore itself generated) -- but it is stated ONLY in a source doc comment.

docs/reference/cli-contract.md:33-38 is where a consumer looks, and it says log.md is "generated output refreshed from git history by lore sync", that it renders each documentation commit once, and that it is outside lore check's drift gate. It says NOTHING about what happens to content already in the file. A reader can reasonably infer "refreshed from git history" means new entries are added; nothing tells them their prose is dropped.

EVIDENCE THIS GAP IS REAL AND COSTLY, 2026-09-13: a consumer's validation suite asserted that arbitrary authored prose in the generated log would survive a sync. It does not, so the test failed, and the failure was reported as 0.6.1 not fixing the LCLI-474 clobbering defect. That report consumed investigation across THREE repositories -- purpose-built fixtures here, an independent non-reproduction by opum-cli-e2e, a third by opum-agent -- plus a serious proposal to provision a Windows CI runner to chase a platform hypothesis that turned out to be irrelevant. The consumer found and corrected their own expectation. Nobody was wrong about the code; the disagreement was about what the generated log PROMISES. See LCLI-484 for the full trail.

The false alarm is the evidence for this task. A documented contract, or a warning at sync time, would have caught it in one step instead of a round trip through three repositories.

acceptanceCriteria.text: docs/reference/cli-contract.md's docs/log.md paragraph states explicitly that the file is regenerated from git history plus the entries still parseable in it, and that any other content -- hand-authored prose, stray edits, the title line, blanks -- is NOT preserved across a sync

The doc says this is deliberate and gives the reason (a total parse degrades to 'carry forward what is still legible' rather than failing the sync and leaving a repo unable to run lore sync at all), so a reader does not file it as a defect

`lore sync` warns when docs/log.md contains unrecognised content that will be dropped, naming at least the count -- so a consumer learns at sync time rather than after a round trip through three repositories

`lore sync` reports a log summary: entries added, carried forward, and dropped. This is the part that would have made the LCLI-484 false alarm self-diagnosing, because the consumer would have seen the drop count move
A test covers the drop-and-warn path, so the documented contract and the implemented one cannot silently diverge later

finalSummary:
Both halves delivered, and the noise trap that would have made the warning useless was avoided.

THE DEFECT: parseEntries is total by construction, so any line that is neither a folder heading nor an entry is skipped silently. A consumer lost authored prose that way and could only discover it by diffing -- the silence was the defect, not the dropping.

DOCUMENTATION HALF (#25). docs/reference/cli-contract.md now states that a sync rebuilds docs/log.md from exactly two inputs -- commits visible in history, and entries still parseable on disk -- that nothing else survives, and that this is deliberate, with the reason: a total parse degrades to 'carry forward what is legible' rather than failing the command and leaving a repository unable to run lore sync because of a file lore itself generated. Placed as preamble paragraphs rather than a new heading, because every ### in that document is numbered under a numbered ## and inserting one would renumber sections 1-8 that other documents cite by number. Verified against the source rather than the prose: FOLDER_HEADING is /^## (\S.*)$/ and LOG_ENTRY is /^- (\S+) (\S+)(?: (.*))?$/, exactly the forms documented.

SOURCE HALF. lore sync now warns when regeneration would drop unrecognised lines, naming the count and sampling the text, and reports 'N added, N carried forward, N dropped' on every sync (also in --json). The warning goes to stderr before the write, and fires on --dry-run too.

THE PART THAT MATTERED MOST, and it is why this was briefed rather than left to discovery: blank lines and the '# Change log' title are skipped by the SAME continue as genuine prose. A naive 'count what was skipped' fires on every sync of every healthy bundle, becomes noise, and gets ignored -- worse than no warning, because it trains people to ignore it. The shipped predicate treats blanks and any level-1 ATX heading as structure and never reports them, and deliberately reports two cases a naive predicate misses: a well-formed entry line with no folder heading above it (nothing to belong to, genuinely lost) and a folder heading whose section yields no entries (a generated log never emits an empty section, so it is hand-authored). Under-reporting a stray '#' is cheap; crying wolf is not.

BYTE IDENTITY WAS A HARD CONSTRAINT and is satisfied by construction, verified by reading the diff rather than trusting the claim: generateLog is now a one-line wrapper returning generateLogWithStats(...).bytes, and the bytes expression is character-for-character unchanged. No existing caller or test changed; the only deletion in the test files is an import line. Downstream repeated-sync byte stability is therefore untouched.

VERIFIED: bun run lint (one warning, the pre-existing src/commands/agents.ts:216, still the only one), bun run typecheck clean, bun test 2933 pass / 1 skip / 0 fail, lore check 77 files 0 errors exit 0. The implementer also mutation-tested the predicate -- forcing isStructural to return false fails 10 assertions across both test files -- which is what shows the tests pin the behaviour rather than restating the plumbing.

ORIGIN: filed out of LCLI-484, where a consumer's suite asserted authored prose would survive a sync. The failing test was reported as a defect in a released fix and investigated across three repositories, plus a serious proposal to provision a Windows CI runner, before the expectation was found to be outside the contract. The false alarm is the evidence for this task: a documented contract, or a warning at sync time, would have ended it in one step.
